description.narrative:
Ongoing hostilities have led to an extremely critical humanitarian situation in Gaza, with more than 40,000 people killed and more than 90,000 injured. According to the latest figures of the UN, 1.9 million people are estimated to be internally displaced within Gaza (90 per cent of the population), with many multiple times. The latest IPC analysis, conducted between 27 May and 4 June 2024, reported that a high and sustained risk of Famine persists across the whole Gaza Strip as long as conflict continues and humanitarian access is restricted. In North Gaza and Gaza governorates specifically, 75,000 people (25 percent of the population) are expected to be in IPC Phase 5 (Catastrophe) between mid-June and end of September 2024. Approximately 150,000 people (50 percent of the population in northern governorates) will be in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency).
WFP reported at the end of July that fuel deliveries and ongoing hostilities have severely constrained the ability to operate critical facilities. As of 1 August, only 12 out of 18 bakeries supported by humanitarian partners remain operational across Gaza. The six bakeries in northern Gaza (four in Gaza city and two in North Gaza) are receiving only scarce fuel quantities, which is sufficient to keep them running just a few days at a time. The volume of distributed food assistance, through the distribution of food parcels, bakeries and community kitchens, is currently insufficient to meet the enormous needs and lacks dietary diversity. This is further exacerbated by the scarcity of commercial commodities and high prices, particularly in northern Gaza. According to OCHA the lack of entry of commercial supplies into northern Gaza for nearly three months has resulted in a near total lack of protein sources such as meat and poultry on the local market, with only a few types of locally produced vegetables available at unaffordable prices. Oxfam’s Rapid Gender Analysis, conducted in May 2024, showed that people resort to drastic measures, such as reducing food intake to 1-2 meals per day and consuming less preferred food to cope with the shortage. Some people reported even eating animal feed and offering services in exchange for food. Priority for food is given to pregnant and breastfeeding women,boys, girls, sick family members, and family members with disabilities. Despite this, 90 per cent of pregnant women, breastfeeding women, and young children are still not meeting their minimum nutritional needs. Other observed coping mechanisms includearise in begging and theft due to the absence of law and order. A common challenge faced by both men and women is the lack of income and employment opportunities. Only 2 per cent of females and 9 percent of males among IDP respondents reported havingsome source of paid work. Men are struggling with feelings of inadequacy and hopelessness due to their inability to fulfil the provider role, resulting in psychological stress and triggering GBV in families. Similarly, women are burdened with the responsibilityof providing for their families and face barriers such as lack of job opportunities and financial assistance. In addition, several WROs (Women Rights Organisation) report that GBV has multiplied and span a wide range of forms. There is an increase in child marriages, with girls as young as 13-14 being married off due to concerns about rising cases of rape and sexual harassment. Instances of divorce and abandonment have also increased due to tensions among couples and extreme stress experienced by displaced people. This has led to an increase in female-headed households. A surge in cases of sexual violence, rape and harassment has been observed. Poor privacy and crowding in shelters and WASH facilities contribute to the occurrences.

participating-org.narrative:
Oxfam Novib has been active in the Occupied Palestinian Territory/Israel (OPT/I) since 1982 and working with Palestinian refugees in Lebanon since the mid 1980s. It has built up a strong network of relationships with local NGOs and counts among its localcounterparts some of the largest and most professional NGOs in various sectors. It has accompanied these NGOs in their development from ad hoc volunteer groups to sizeable professional institutions with national outreach. At the same time the conceptualisation of the programme has evolved from three country programs in the early 1990s to a program for Palestinians in the Middle East (PME) working withPalestinians in OPT, Israel and Lebanon.
The programme has changed over the years with the establishment of the Palestinian Authority (PA) in the mid-1990s from a focus on support and service provision at a grassroots level and grassroots mobilization, to working towards influencing the establishment of the PA, its lawmaking and supporting building a democratic state # this involved supporting efforts of Palestinian civil society to build the basis for a democratic Palestinian state with room for civil participation, ensuring inclusion of vulnerable groups, refugees and women, and shaping its laws and systems. Oxfam Novib has also supported partners that are working on the provision of humanitarian assistance, response preparedness and conflict transformation. We have also supported partners in the provision of health services, access to quality education and gender justice.
